nameStory: Common hibiscus is widely known as 'rose of Sharon,' a name that creates endless confusion since it's neither a rose nor native to Sharon! The name likely comes from the Biblical 'rose of Sharon' mentioned in the Song of Solomon, though that probably referred to a completely different Middle Eastern plant. The scientific name 'syriacus' adds to the geographic mix-up, given because early botanists first collected it from Syrian gardens, even though it's actually native to East Asia.
description: Common hibiscus is a deciduous shrub that can grow 8-12 feet tall, creating an upright, somewhat vase-shaped form. It's beloved for its showy, tropical-looking flowers that bloom from mid-summer into fall, each lasting just one day but produced in steady succession. The flowers are typically 3-4 inches across and come in white, pink, purple, or blue, often with darker centers. This hardy shrub is commonly planted in gardens and has naturalized in some areas, making it a familiar sight in New England landscapes.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large, showy flowers with 5 broad petals arranged like a funnel, featuring a prominent central column (pistil and stamens fused together) that sticks out noticeably. The petals feel papery-thin and delicate to the touch, and flowers often have a darker red or purple eye in the center.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-lobed leaves that are roughly triangular with coarse teeth along the edges, feeling somewhat rough and dry to the touch. They're arranged alternately along the stems and turn yellow before dropping in fall.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, multi-stemmed shrub with gray-brown bark that develops shallow furrows on older stems. Young branches feel smooth and slightly flexible, while mature wood becomes quite sturdy.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dry, brown seed capsules about the size of a large pea that split open when ripe, revealing small dark seeds inside. The capsules persist into winter and rattle when shaken.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Small, pointed buds pressed close to the stem in winter, covered in brown scales. The buds have no particular scent when crushed, unlike some shrubs.

habitat: Common hibiscus thrives in full sun and well-drained soils, commonly found in suburban gardens, park plantings, and along roadsides where it has escaped cultivation. It tolerates urban conditions well and can naturalize in disturbed areas, field edges, and sunny woodland borders. Look for it in residential areas, commercial landscapes, and occasionally in wild spaces near human development.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, unfolding as bright green, three-lobed shapes. The shrub leafs out later than many other plants, sometimes causing gardeners to worry it didn't survive winter.
seasonality.summer: The spectacular flowering season begins in mid to late summer, with large, colorful blooms opening daily from July through September. Each flower lasts only one day but new buds keep the show going for weeks.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow before dropping, and brown seed capsules become prominent. The flowering may continue into early fall if weather stays warm.
seasonality.winter: Bare gray-brown stems with small, tight buds and persistent seed capsules that rattle in the wind. The multi-stemmed, upright silhouette is distinctive against snow.

funFact: Each gorgeous hibiscus flower lives for exactly one day – opening in the morning and closing forever by evening, which is why it's sometimes called the 'daily hibiscus.' A single healthy shrub can produce hundreds of these one-day wonders over the course of a summer, creating what looks like a continuous bloom but is actually a parade of individual flowers each having their brief moment of glory!
confusionNotes: The large, tropical-looking flowers make this pretty unmistakable when blooming, but the three-lobed leaves might be confused with maple seedlings. Remember: maples have opposite leaves while hibiscus has alternate leaves, plus maple leaves feel thinner and more delicate.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'rose of Sharon,' this plant is completely unrelated to roses and has nothing to do with the biblical land of Sharon. It's actually South Korea's national flower and is mentioned in their national anthem. The abundance of common names (Syrian ketmia, shrub althea, Korean rose) reflects its long history in gardens worldwide and the confusion about its origins.
compareHints: Common hibiscus differs from its native relative swamp rose mallow by being a woody shrub rather than an herbaceous perennial, and having smaller flowers with three-lobed leaves instead of large heart-shaped ones. Swamp rose mallow also prefers wet areas and has much larger flowers (6-8 inches across), while common hibiscus thrives in average garden conditions with more modest but still showy blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Swamp rose mallow differs from the common garden hibiscus (rose-of-Sharon) by its much larger flowers, fuzzy leaves, and wetland habitat – rose-of-Sharon has smaller flowers and smooth leaves and grows in dry garden conditions.
Unlike its New England hibiscus relatives such as swamp rose mallow with its huge pink flowers or common hibiscus with its large shrubby form, flower-of-an-hour stays small and annual.
Scarlet rosemallow stands out from its hibiscus relatives by its intense red flower color and deeply divided, almost star-shaped leaves.
